After the May quake, the Alberta Energy Regulator said it had received no reports of damage or injuries. Researchers have now traced both earthquakes to carbon dioxide injected at Alberta's Quest storage project.

Science.title: Why a warmer atmosphere doesn't guarantee more water in rivers
Science.summary: Austria experienced an exceptional drought in 2026. From the start of the year until the end of October, rainfall was around a third lower than the long-term average. The consequences are low river flows and groundwater levels. But how is water availability linked to global warming? Shouldn't a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more water vapor, also lead to more rainfall?

Science.title: The world is experiencing a string of abnormally hot days—and records are being shattered
Science.summary: We're becoming used to seeing records being broken whenever we look at data telling us about Earth's climate. Whether it's the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, heat in the ocean or shrinking sea ice around the poles, the signs of human-caused climate change are all around us.

Science.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
Science.summary: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

Science.title: Study shows path to more resilient future for Canada's forests
Science.summary: Mountain pine beetles have killed millions of lodgepole pines across western North America since the 1990s, but some trees have proved more resilient than others. New research suggests part of the difference is genetic and that the resistance can be passed from one generation of trees to the next.

Science.title: Denisovan remains and an unknown archaic human lineage discovered in southern China
Science.summary: An international team of researchers, including first author Song Xing, a researcher affiliated with the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH), has just published a study in the journal Nature that analyzed four fossil teeth recovered from two caves in southern China. The team has identified two possible human lineages dating to the Middle and Late Pleistocene: one with Denisovan affinities and another more primitive lineage whose evolutionary identity remains unclear.

Science.title: Melting Barents Sea ice gives Eastern Europe's farmers a spring boost
Science.summary: For decades, sea ice in the Barents Sea, a part of the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia, has been shrinking as the Arctic warms. The loss of so much ice can alter weather patterns well beyond the polar region, including in Europe. But how these changes might affect vegetation growth and agricultural production is less well understood.

Science.title: When bad weather hits a fragile financial system
Science.summary: An extreme weather event does more than just destroy buildings, facilities or infrastructure. It can also reduce the value of collateral, weaken banks, make credit more expensive and force businesses to postpone investment. Consequently, the damage risks spreading well beyond the locality where the event occurred.

Science.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
Science.summary: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity.

Science.title: Antarctic sea ice extent hits new low
Science.summary: Satellite observations show Antarctic sea ice coverage dipped to record daily lows in October 2026, surpassing even the extremely low extent observed in October 2023—the year poor sea ice conditions led to the deaths of thousands of emperor penguin chicks in Antarctica.

Science.title: DARPA is assessing Microsoft's controversial quantum computing technology. What will happen if the Majorana 2 platform is vindicated?
Science.summary: Microsoft has doubled down on its Majorana 2 quantum computing platform despite pushback from the physics community, with DARPA researchers now set to evaluate the bold claims.

Science.title: Is AI‑assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?
Science.summary: As AI models improve, high-quality knowledge is becoming easier to access. A degree therefore has to certify something more durable than the ability to retrieve knowledge or produce a plausible answer. It must show that a student can exercise judgment, make decisions and defend them.

Science.title: Audio long read: The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03900-8 Rare neurons taken from living humans are helping researchers test how brain cells behave in their natural environment.

Science.title: Lab experiments suggest bat RSV can enter human cells, but existing antibodies block it
Science.summary: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes severe respiratory disease and is responsible for numerous deaths each year. A research team led by DZIF scientist Dr. Wendy K. Jo and DZIF scientist Dr. Jan Felix Drexler at Charité—University Medicine Berlin, as well as DZIF board member Dr. Thomas Pietschmann and Dr. Sibylle Haid from TWINCORE in Hanover, has now characterized a virus in West African fruit bats that is genetically distinct from known RSV variants but belongs to the same viral family as RSV.

Science.title: AI could be used to write your child's report. Is this a problem?
Science.summary: For many families, it's that time of year when school reports land in parents' inboxes.

Science.title: James Webb telescope discovers mysterious red object just 450 million years after the Big Bang — and it could be a baby black hole
Science.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has spotted a tiny, extremely red object in the infant universe. It may be one of the earliest black holes, but researchers can't yet rule out a very different explanation.

Science.title: Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam's tropical forests isn't guaranteed
Science.summary: Deep in the jungle of central Vietnam, the heat is heavy, the mosquitoes are relentless and the terrain offers no easy paths. My colleagues and I don't hike on clear trails; we wade up riverbeds, stepping carefully over slippery rocks to access the thousands of trees we have been measuring for the last decade.

Science.title: Make the most of the new moon on Dec. 8 and get closer views of the stars with the Celestron Inspire 100AZ
Science.summary: The Celestron Inspire 100AZ is a great first telescope and will give you better views of the stars and Saturn in the moonless skies come Dec. 8. It is now 15% cheaper for Black Friday.

Science.title: Newly discovered barrier could explain why nucleic acid medicines remain trapped inside cells
Science.summary: Researchers from the Department of Chemistry at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) and their collaborators have discovered a barrier that may prevent some promising nucleic acid medicines from reaching their targets inside subcellular compartments. Published in Nature Cell Biology, the findings could help guide the development of more effective drug delivery strategies.

Science.title: New technologies help Natural History Museum uncover 92 species in its transformed gardens
Science.summary: The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

Science.title: Brain area’s mysterious role in speech decoded at last
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03800-x Wernicke’s area is known for processing spoken words, but brain recordings reveal that it also makes a crucial contribution to a related cognitive task.

Science.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
Science.summary: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?

Science.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
Science.summary: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

Science.title: Strawberries, cucumbers and lemon basil show promise for future moon and Mars menus
Science.summary: As NASA prepares for future missions to the moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Science.title: Engineers reveal the interlayer elastic limits of van der Waals crystals
Science.summary: A research team led by Professor Yang Lu from the Department of Mechanical Engineering in the Faculty of Engineering at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), in collaboration with Tsinghua University, has measured the interlayer elastic limits of graphite and hexagonal boron nitride, two representative van der Waals crystals, and revealed the physical mechanism that sets them. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

Science.title: Why are we the last humans standing? What interbreeding with Neanderthals reveals about the differences between us.
Science.summary: In this exclusive video, Live Science explores what ancient DNA reveals about the relationships between Neanderthals and modern humans.

Science.title: Love Star Wars, Andy Weir or Ryan Gosling? These Lego Star Wars and Project Hail Mary sets are my favorites
Science.summary: Whether you're a fan of Star Wars, Ryan Gosling or both, you're spoilt for choice this Black Friday with serious savings on Lego's Star Wars sets and Project Hail Mary sets.

Science.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
Science.summary: A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.

Science.title: Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03754-0 Studies are more likely to be cited in patents if they are freely available — legitimately or otherwise — researchers have found.

Science.title: Rocks under the lens: A simple microscope opens new possibilities for quantitative rock analysis
Science.summary: Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

Science.title: Life-saving cancer drug pumped out by a plant
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03801-w In a proof-of-concept study, scientists have coaxed a tobacco-related plant to synthesize the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel.

Science.title: Postcards from your graves
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03523-z A disastrous outcome.

Science.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
Science.summary: Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

Science.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
Science.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

Science.title: Work-life balance predicts job satisfaction more strongly than pay or flexible working in study
Science.summary: Work-life balance has a stronger association with job satisfaction than pay or flexible working arrangements, according to a study of employees in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) published in the International Journal of Economics and Business Research.

Science.title: New research establishes fundamental complexity limit for quantum circuit optimization
Science.summary: Quantum circuit optimization is an important research area, as the computational resources required to execute quantum algorithms remain a major challenge. In particular, two-qubit operations are generally associated with higher error rates than single-qubit gates on current quantum hardware, making reducing the number of two-qubit gates an important objective.

Science.title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
Science.summary: Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her workday with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

Science.title: Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst
Science.summary: Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials.

Science.title: The haunting loveliness of boglands: Books in brief
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03885-4 Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

Science.title: Income inequality is rising while becoming more similar across countries
Science.summary: Inequality is a much-debated issue in politics and society. International comparative research shows that income inequality has risen in most countries. At the same time, however, the differences in disposable income levels between countries have narrowed.

Science.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
Science.summary: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

Science.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
Science.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

Science.title: Can storybook characters teach children about perseverance?
Science.summary: Many storybooks incorporate messages about not giving up when faced with a challenge—something that perhaps isn't surprising given that perseverance is an important factor for learning and long-term success.

Science.title: NASA’s NG-25 Mission to Launch Pioneering Space Crops Research
Science.summary: NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency. Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health. Groundbreaking […]

Science.title: Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact
Science.summary: Arriving at the site of humankind's first planetary defense experiment, the European Space Agency's Hera mission has found a miniature world of surprises. Dimorphos—the small asteroid whose orbit around a second, larger asteroid was deflected by a spacecraft impact—now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically. Meanwhile, hundreds of previously unknown boulders encircle the binary pair.

Science.title: Artemis III Astronaut Andre Douglas Visits VAB
Science.summary: NASA astronaut Andre Douglas, Artemis III mission specialist, stands inside an RS-25 engine test article during a visit to the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. During Artemis III, four RS-25 engines will power the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket core stage to send the Orion […]
